questions.text: A 5 sq.m detached tool shed in a residential backyard and a 20 sq.m bamboo house costing P12,000 for a caretaker are being planned. Under PD 1096, which statement is legally accurate?

options.text: Both structures require a building permit but neither requires payment of fees, as they fall under exemptions for small structures
The tool shed is exempt from a permit; the bamboo house requires a permit but is exempt from fees
The bamboo house is exempt from a permit; the tool shed requires a permit and fees, due to its specific use and construction type
Neither structure requires a building permit, as both are considered minor structures under the building code

questions.rationale: This is the single most important distinction in the entire permit exemptions topic. Fee exemptions (Sec. 209) still require a permit — only the fee payment is waived. Permit exemptions (Sec. 301.3) mean no permit is needed at all. These are two entirely separate lists with different criteria. Option A reverses both. Option C swaps the two exemptions. Option D applies permit exemption to the bamboo house incorrectly.

questions.text: Table VIII.1 provides which of the following?

options.text: Front, side, and rear yard setback distances, which are essential for ensuring adequate space between structures
PSO, ISA, USA, and TOSL values by occupancy and lot type
Building Height Limits by occupancy group, which are critical for maintaining urban skyline consistency
FLAR designations by zone classification, which help in determining the allowable floor area ratio for developments

questions.rationale: The three setback tables: Table VIII.1 = PSO/ISA/USA/TOSL; Table VIII.2 = Residential setbacks by zone; Table VIII.3 = Non-residential setbacks by RROW width. Each table serves a different function.

questions.text: Under Table VIII.3 of the 2004 Revised IRR, what is the minimum front setback for a commercial building on a 30-meter-wide RROW?
questions.rationale: The non-residential setback table (VIII.3) is keyed by RROW width, not by zoning density — a critical distinction from the residential table. Wider roads justify wider front setbacks.

questions.text: What is the minimum easement zone from a riverbank in an urban area, according to PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines) Article 51?

options.text: 3.00 m from the riverbank
10.00 m from the riverbank
20.00 m from the riverbank
1.00 m per meter of water width, up to 3.00 m maximum

questions.rationale: The 3/20/40 m easements are a high-frequency exam topic. Always deduct the applicable easement strip from the lot's buildable dimension based on the site's land classification (urban/agricultural/forest), not the width of the water body.

questions.text: Under Table VIII.2 of the 2004 Revised IRR, what is the minimum front setback for an R-1 (single-family) lot?
questions.rationale: R-1 is the most restrictive single-family zone. Its 4.50 m front setback is larger than R-2 Basic (3.00 m) or R-3 Basic (3.00 m) to preserve the character of low-density residential areas.

questions.text: Under Table VIII.3, what are the front, side, and rear setbacks for a commercial building on an RROW of 10.00–19.00 m width?

options.text: 5.00 m front, 2.00 m side, 2.00 m rear
5.00 m front, 2.00 m side, 3.00 m rear
8.00 m front, 5.00 m side, 5.00 m rear
5.00 m front, 3.00 m side, 3.00 m rear

questions.rationale: The side and rear setbacks are consistent at 2.00 m across all RROW bands from 10.00 m and above. Only the front setback increases with wider RROW.

questions.text: What is the minimum easement from a shoreline in an agricultural area, per PD 1067 Article 51?

options.text: 3.00 m from the mean high tide line
20.00 m from the mean high tide line
40.00 m from the mean high tide line
100.00 m from the shoreline

questions.rationale: The three values (3/20/40 m) apply to ALL bodies of water (rivers, streams, seas, lakes) — the variable is the land classification (urban/agricultural/forest), not the water body type.

questions.text: Under PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines), Article 51, what is the required public-use easement zone along a riverbank in an urban area?

options.text: 3.00 m from the riverbank in urban areas
10.00 m from the riverbank regardless of land classification
20.00 m from the riverbank in urban areas
1.00 m per meter of water width, up to 3.00 m maximum

questions.rationale: PD 1067 Article 51 establishes: banks of rivers and streams are subject to a public-use easement of 3.00 m in urban areas, 20.00 m in agricultural areas, and 40.00 m in forest areas. The variable is the land classification of the bank — not the width of the water body. The common distractor '1 m per meter of water width' does not appear in Article 51. Mnemonic: '3–20–40 along the water' (urban/agri/forest).
questions.explanation: These buffer strips ensure public access to waterways and provide safety margins against flooding and shoreline erosion. Always deduct the easement from the lot's buildable dimension based on site land classification, not water body type or width.
questions.code_citation: PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines), Article 51

questions.text: Under Rule VIII, Sec. 804, how many sides of an R-1 lot may have abutments (walls built at zero setback on the property line)?

options.text: One side only — the same rule as R-2, which allows limited abutment for privacy
Two sides — the same rule as R-3 and R-4, reflecting higher density allowances
None — abutments are absolutely prohibited on R-1 lots on any property line
Any side, subject to Building Official approval on a case-by-case basis, allowing flexibility in design

questions.rationale: Abutments are absolutely prohibited in R-1. No abutments are allowed on any property line of an R-1 lot. This preserves the fully detached character of single-family dwellings and ensures complete light, ventilation, and fire separation on all sides. By contrast: R-2 allows one side abutment; R-3 allows two sides or one side plus rear; R-4 allows two sides; R-5 allows two sides or one side plus rear.
questions.explanation: The zero-abutment rule for R-1 is absolute — no exceptions or BO waivers. The progression from R-1 (none) to R-3/R-5 (two sides or one side plus rear) reflects increasing urban density and the corresponding reduction in required separation between adjacent structures.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule VIII, Section 804, Table VIII.2 (2004 Revised IRR)

questions.text: Under Rule VIII, Sec. 804, Sub. 6, at what rate does the minimum rear or side court width increase for buildings above 2 storeys, and at what storey does the increment cap?

options.text: 200 mm per storey above the 2nd, capped at the 12th storey
300 mm per storey above the 2nd, capped at the 14th storey
500 mm per storey above the 1st, capped at the 10th storey
250 mm per storey above the 2nd, capped at the 20th storey

questions.rationale: Per Sec. 804, Sub. 6, the minimum width of the required rear or side court increases by 300 mm per storey above the 2nd storey, up to the 14th storey. The increment caps at 14 storeys — for buildings taller than 14 storeys, use the width computed for the 14th storey. Worked example: 10-storey building, base side setback 3.00 m, RROW 25 m. Additional storeys = 10 − 2 = 8. Increment = 8 × 0.30 = 2.40 m. Total = 3.00 + 2.40 = 5.40 m.
questions.explanation: Taller buildings block more sky and air, so courts must grow proportionally to retain light and ventilation. The 14-storey cap prevents courts from growing unreasonably large for supertall buildings while ensuring adequate light access for mid-rise and high-rise structures.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule VIII, Section 804, Subsection 6 (2004 Revised IRR)

questions.text: Under Rule X, Sec. 1002(2), what are the maximum projection and minimum depth for a building footing along a national road?

options.text: Maximum 300 mm projection, at least 2.40 m below grade
Maximum 500 mm projection, at least 600 mm below grade
Maximum 200 mm projection, at least 1.80 m below grade
Maximum 600 mm projection, at least 3.00 m below grade

questions.rationale: Rule X, Sec. 1002(2) governs footings along national roads: maximum projection of 300 mm beyond the property line, at a minimum depth of 2.40 m below grade. This is one of two distinct underground projection rules — do not confuse it with Sec. 1002(3) which governs foundations into sidewalks (500 mm encroachment, 600 mm below grade). Mnemonic: 'F-3-2' — Footing (300 mm, 2.40 m depth).
questions.explanation: The two underground rules apply to different elements in different locations: Sec. 1002(2) = footing along national road (300 mm / 2.40 m deep); Sec. 1002(3) = foundation into sidewalk (500 mm / 600 mm deep). Merging them into a single table is a common study error.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule X, Section 1002(2)

questions.text: Under Rule X, Sec. 1002(3), what are the maximum encroachment width and minimum depth for a foundation projecting into a public sidewalk?

options.text: Maximum 300 mm encroachment, top of foundation at least 2.40 m below grade
Maximum 500 mm encroachment, top of foundation at least 600 mm below grade
Maximum 600 mm encroachment, top of foundation at least 500 mm below grade
Maximum 500 mm encroachment, top of foundation at least 1.20 m below grade

questions.rationale: Rule X, Sec. 1002(3) governs foundations into public sidewalks: maximum encroachment width of 500 mm, with the top of the foundation at least 600 mm below established grade. Sidewalks carry utilities at shallow depths, so the foundation must stay below them while allowing limited horizontal encroachment. Mnemonic: 'F-5-6' — Foundation (500 mm encroachment, 600 mm depth to top).
questions.explanation: The sidewalk foundation rule (500 mm / 600 mm) is less deep than the national road footing rule (300 mm / 2.40 m) because sidewalk utilities are shallower than road subbase. Both rules also require that utilities must not be obstructed unless the owner pays rerouting costs.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule X, Section 1002(3)

questions.text: Under Rule X, what are the minimum vertical clearances above grade for a balcony and for a movable awning respectively?

options.text: Balcony: 2.40 m; Awning: 3.00 m
Balcony: 3.00 m; Awning: 3.00 m
Balcony: 3.00 m; Awning: 2.40 m
Balcony: 2.40 m; Awning: 2.40 m

questions.rationale: Per Rule X Sec. 1003, balconies and appendages require a minimum vertical clearance of 3.00 m above grade. Per Sec. 1006, movable awnings require a minimum vertical clearance of 2.40 m above pavement. The common trap is reversing the values. Mnemonic: 'Permanent = 3.00; movable = 2.40.' Canopies (permanent marquees, Sec. 1005) also require 3.00 m, same as balconies.
questions.explanation: The 3.00 m clearance for permanent overhead structures ensures full pedestrian and vehicle headroom beneath. The reduced 2.40 m for movable awnings reflects their retractable nature and lower structural permanence. Doors and windows below 2.40 m may not project beyond the property line (Sec. 1007).
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule X, Sections 1003 and 1006

questions.text: The 2004 Revised IRR identifies how many standardized lot types, and which lot type has the lowest Total Open Space within Lot (TOSL) requirement?

options.text: 5 lot types; Through Lots have the lowest TOSL requirement, which is advantageous for maximizing buildable area
7 lot types; Corner-Through Lots and Corner lots abutting 3 or more streets have the lowest TOSL (approximately 5% for all groups)
6 lot types; Corner Lots have the lowest TOSL requirement, allowing for more efficient land use
8 lot types; Interior Lots have the lowest TOSL requirement, which is contrary to typical zoning practices

questions.rationale: The IRR identifies 7 standardized lot configurations: Interior Lot, Inside Lot, Corner Lot, Through Lot, Corner-Through Lot, End Lot, and Corner Lot abutting 3 or more streets/alleys/rivers. The Corner-Through Lot and Corner lot abutting 3 or more streets have the lowest TOSL — approximately 5% for all occupancy groups — because maximum public frontage provides the greatest natural light and ventilation access from the surroundings.
questions.explanation: The logic is inverse: the more public frontages a lot has, the more light and air it receives from its surroundings, so the less internal open space it needs to provide. Interior lots (only one frontage) require the highest TOSL — 50% for Groups A–D, J or 20% for Groups E–I. Corner-through lots (three frontages) require only about 5% for all groups.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule VIII, Section 804, Figures VIII.2–VIII.8 (2004 Revised IRR)

questions.text: Under Rule X, Sec. 1008, when is a chaflan (corner chamfer) required on a corner building, and what is the exemption?

options.text: Required on all corner buildings regardless of street width; no exemption exists, which is a strict interpretation of the rule.
Required when the corner building is on a street or alley less than 3.60 m wide; exempt if the corner building is arcaded
Required only when building height exceeds 15.00 m on a corner lot, which is a condition that considers both height and location.
Required for all commercial corner buildings; residential corner buildings are exempt, which differentiates based on building use.

questions.rationale: Rule X, Sec. 1008 requires chamfering (chaflan) of the corner when a building or solid fence occupies a corner on a street or alley less than 3.60 m wide. The face of the chamfer triangle is at right angles to the bisector of the intersection angle. Exemption: if the corner building is arcaded, the chaflan is not required even when the street is less than 3.60 m wide. Chaflans open sight lines at tight corners for vehicles and pedestrians.
questions.explanation: The 3.60 m threshold reflects the minimum turning clearance for a vehicle. Narrower streets with blind corners are particularly dangerous for pedestrians and motorcycles. The arcade exemption works because an arcade already creates a setback from the corner, effectively performing the same visual-clearance function as a chaflan.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule X, Section 1008

questions.text: Under Table VIII.2 of the 2004 Revised IRR, what is the minimum front setback for an R-1 (single-family) residential lot?

options.text: 3.00 m — same as the basic front setback for R-2 and R-3 Basic
4.50 m — the largest default front yard among residential zones
6.00 m — required for the lowest-density single-detached zone
8.00 m — same as the front setback for commercial buildings on wide roads

questions.rationale: Per Table VIII.2, the minimum front setback for R-1 is 4.50 m. Students frequently confuse this with the 3.00 m basic front setback of R-2 and R-3. R-1 is the lowest-density single-detached zone and receives the largest default front yard among residential classifications. Mnemonic: 'R-1 = 4 and a half, R-2/3 Basic = 3 flat.'
questions.explanation: R-1 front setback: 4.50 m. R-2 Basic front setback: 3.00 m. R-5 front setback: 6.00 m. The setback increases with zoning density — the highest-density R-5 zone requires the largest 6.00 m front setback because mixed-use buildings there are treated as commercial.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule VIII, Table VIII.2 (2004 Revised IRR)

questions.text: Under Table VIII.3 of the 2004 Revised IRR, what are the front, side, and rear setbacks for a commercial building on an RROW of 30 meters or wider?

options.text: Front: 5.00 m; Side: 2.00 m; Rear: 2.00 m
Front: 6.00 m; Side: 3.00 m; Rear: 3.00 m
Front: 8.00 m; Side: 5.00 m; Rear: 5.00 m
Front: 8.00 m; Side: 3.00 m; Rear: 3.00 m

questions.rationale: Per Table VIII.3, for RROW width of 30.00 m and above: front setback = 8.00 m, side setback = 5.00 m, rear setback = 5.00 m. Wider roads carry more traffic and serve a broader urban territory, so buildings on major thoroughfares must step back further. The non-residential setback table is keyed by RROW width — not zoning density.
questions.explanation: The two setback tables use different keys: Table VIII.2 uses residential zoning density (R-1 to R-5); Table VIII.3 uses RROW width for commercial, industrial, institutional, and recreational buildings. Never apply residential setback values to a commercial project.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule VIII, Table VIII.3 (2004 Revised IRR)
